1.text: Maritime Chukchee the men who seem to be quite decrepit almost always

2.text: prove to have become so rather from the hardships of life than from old age.

3.text: Such men are speedily carried away by disease. Therefore the really old men,

4.text: in my opinion, are not numerous.

5.text: THE SENSES. — Of the special senses, smell seems to be more developed

6.text: than with civilized races, since the Chukchee assert that every man has a

7.text: smell peculiar to himself, and that his clothes, etc., can be ascertained from

8.text: it. I was told that in olden times, during the wars among the Koryak, the

9.text: invading Chukchee parties, finding an old camping-place, were able to ascertain,

10.text: from the odor of broken bones and other remains, whether they belonged to

11.text: the Koryak or to their own tribe. Accordingly mutual sniffing has the same

12.text: value as kissing, as is the case with many other primitive tribes. The Chuk-

13.text: chee father, when leaving his family for a trip, will perhaps kiss his wife; but

14.text: he will usually apply his nose to the nape of his children’s necks, and inhale

15.text: the odor of their fur shirts.

16.text: I must note, too, the sensitiveness of the Chukchee to unfamiliar odors.

17.text: Every time that I happened to open my small chest of medicines in a Chuk-

18.text: chee sleeping-room, the inmates complained loudly of the offensive smell which

19.text: came from it, and sometimes I was obliged to go away to the outer tent

20.text: with my patients. Similar complaint was made against some wild onions that

21.text: I brought in, though the Russianized natives use them for food and even

22.text: store them in large quantities for winter use. The Chukchee name for them

24.text: The taboo against bringing into a Chukchee sleeping-room any objects

25.text: connected with the hearths and households of other families is founded, in the

26.text: minds of the people, chiefly upon their unfamiliar odor. I have had some

27.text: curious experiences regarding this idiosyncrasy. In 1896, while travelling among

28.text: the Anui Chukchee, I happened to procure a document of the year 1789;

29.text: acknowledging the loyal faith of a certain Qɪˊmɪqäi, evidently a rich reindeer-

30.text: owner (the document calls him, with the usual misapprehension of the Chuk-

31.text: chee social organization, “Chief of the Chaun Chukchee”). This document

32.text: had been preserved in the family of Qɪˊmɪqäi for more than a century, and

33.text: had gradually come to be considered, along with the fire-drills and strings

34.text: of amulets, a part of their sacred possessions. The family became extinct,

35.text: and I was able to acquire it, together with a curious wooden case adorned

36.text: with beads and tassels, for a moderate price. When I brought it to the tent

37.text: in which I was temporarily living, my host warned me against taking it into

38.text: the inner room; but as it was bitterly cold outside, and as I wished to examine

39.text: the paper, I took it in. No sooner had I produced the fatal wooden case

40.text: from my bag, than the mistress of the house, a sickly woman of thirty, who

41.text: sat opposite me, nursing a child on her lap, moaned and fell senseless. We

42.text: had much trouble in reviving her, and afterwards I had to expiate my offence
